t: Ovary and fallopian tube: cysts, adnexal masses and tumors
sub: Sort an adnexal mass by age, ultrasound and marker, then name the ovarian cell it came from and the way it behaves.

pretest.q: Which ovarian neoplasm is most common in women under 30?
pretest.why: The mature cystic teratoma, or dermoid cyst, is the most common ovarian neoplasm in young women. It is benign, holds tissue from all three germ layers such as hair, teeth and sebum, and its weight makes the ovary prone to torsion.

w.Serous carcinoma: Serous carcinoma is the most common malignant ovarian tumor overall, but it mainly affects women after menopause and BRCA carriers.
w.Granulosa cell tumor: Granulosa cell tumors are uncommon sex cord-stromal tumors, most often seen around or after menopause with estrogen effects such as bleeding.
w.Brenner tumor: Brenner tumors are uncommon, usually benign epithelial tumors of transitional-type cells, typically found incidentally in older women.

pretest.q: Which serum marker does a yolk sac tumor secrete?
pretest.why: Yolk sac tissue makes alpha-fetoprotein in the embryo, so a yolk sac tumor, a malignant germ cell tumor of girls and young women, raises serum AFP and shows glomerulus-like Schiller-Duval bodies.

w.Inhibin: Inhibin is made by granulosa cells, so it marks granulosa cell tumors, which are sex cord-stromal rather than germ cell tumors.
w.CA-125: CA-125 comes from coelomic-type epithelium and rises with epithelial ovarian cancers, especially high-grade serous carcinoma, and with benign pelvic conditions.
w.Lactate dehydrogenase: Lactate dehydrogenase is the marker of dysgerminoma, the ovarian counterpart of seminoma, which grows as sheets of clear cells.

pretest.q: In ovarian torsion, which vessels are compressed first?
pretest.why: Veins and lymphatics have thin walls and low pressure, so twisting collapses them first while arterial blood keeps entering. The ovary swells with congestion and edema before arterial flow stops and infarction follows.

w.Ovarian artery: The ovarian artery has a thick muscular wall and high pressure, so it keeps delivering blood until swelling and further twisting finally occlude it.
w.Uterine artery: The uterine artery supplies the uterus and anastomoses with the ovarian artery, but it is not the vessel twisted in the infundibulopelvic ligament.
w.Internal iliac artery: The internal iliac artery lies on the pelvic sidewall far from the twisting pedicle, so torsion does not compress it.

body: Is an adnexal mass a cyst of ovulation or a true tumor?

The adnexa are the ovary, the fallopian tube and the tissue around them, so a mass there is not always ovarian. A hydrosalpinx (a tube swollen with fluid after salpingitis), a tubo-ovarian abscess, a paratubal cyst and an ectopic pregnancy can all form one, so a pregnancy test comes first in any woman of reproductive age. Most ovarian masses in young women are **functional** cysts, exaggerations of the normal cycle that shrink or vanish on a repeat scan within one to three cycles, whereas a mass that persists, grows or has solid parts is a neoplasm until proven otherwise.

A {{rp15_folcyst|follicular cyst}}, the most common, forms when a follicle fails to rupture and keeps filling with fluid. A **corpus luteum cyst** forms after ovulation, and when it bleeds it becomes a **hemorrhagic cyst** that causes sudden one-sided pain and can rupture with blood in the pelvis. **Theca lutein cysts** are usually bilateral and multiloculated; very high hCG from a molar pregnancy, twins or ovarian hyperstimulation overstimulates the theca cells, and the cysts regress once hCG falls.
What does the ultrasound show, and how is risk scored?

Transvaginal ultrasound is the first test. The uterus shows an **endometrial stripe**, a thin line at menses and a thick bright band in the secretory phase; in a postmenopausal woman with bleeding, a stripe of 4 mm or less makes endometrial cancer unlikely. The cervix carries the endocervical canal as a thin bright line. Each ovary is an oval organ whose cortex holds round **antral follicles**. Fluid is **anechoic**: it returns no echoes and looks black, so follicles, simple cysts and free fluid are black, while solid tissue is gray to white.

Each common benign mass has its own echo pattern. A **simple cyst** is unilocular (one cavity), thin-walled and anechoic, with no flow; in a young woman it is almost always benign and needs only expectant management with a repeat scan. A hemorrhagic cyst has lace-like, reticular echoes and a retracting clot, with no flow inside. An endometrioma, a cyst of endometriosis that causes pain and infertility, has uniform **ground-glass** echoes from old blood. A dermoid has a bright {{rp15_rok|Rokitansky nodule}} (the dermoid plug) with a shadow behind it. A twisted ovary is large and edematous, with follicles pushed to its edge, and its pedicle forms a **whirlpool** sign.

Malignancy is suggested by features that make a mass less like a cyst: a **solid component**, papillary projections (solid nodules growing from the wall), thick septations, flow inside solid tissue and ascites. Architecture counts too: a **multilocular cyst** with septations is riskier than a unilocular one, and an irregular wall or septum is riskier than a smooth one. Flow is graded as the **color score**, from 1 (none) to 4 (very strong). The {{rp15_orads|O-RADS}} ultrasound system turns these findings into risk categories.
Simple cyst; typical hemorrhagic cyst, dermoid or endometrioma under 10 cm
Smooth multilocular cyst under 10 cm; larger typical benign lesions
Irregular or very large multilocular cyst; cyst with a few papillary projections; solid mass with moderate flow
At least four papillary projections; irregular solid mass; ascites or peritoneal nodularity

The IOTA Simple Rules pair five benign features (such as a unilocular cyst or no flow) with five malignant ones (such as an irregular solid mass, ascites or at least four papillary projections). Only benign features means benign, only malignant features means malignant, and any mixture is inconclusive. The **risk of malignancy index** multiplies the ultrasound score, the menopausal score (1 before menopause, 3 after) and the CA-125; above 200 prompts referral to a gynecologic oncologist.
Who gets which mass, and how is it managed?
Germ cell tumors (dermoid, yolk sac, dysgerminoma); torsion
Ultrasound with AFP, hCG and LDH
Functional cysts, endometrioma, dermoid, ectopic pregnancy, hydrosalpinx, tubo-ovarian abscess
Epithelial carcinoma until proven otherwise; fibroma, granulosa tumor
Ultrasound features plus CA-125; refer a complex mass
How an adnexal mass is worked up and managed
Check hCG first in reproductive age; a positive test with a mass suggests ectopic pregnancy. Fever suggests a tubo-ovarian abscess, and sudden one-sided pain with vomiting suggests torsion.
Call the mass simple, classic benign or complex and score it with O-RADS or the Simple Rules; add MRI if indeterminate.
AFP, hCG and LDH for a solid mass in a young patient; CA-125 after menopause or for a suspicious mass; inhibin if the picture is hormonal.

Premenopausal simple or classic benign cysts get expectant management with a repeat scan. A benign mass that persists, grows or hurts, such as a dermoid or endometrioma, is removed by laparoscopic **cystectomy**, which spares ovarian tissue; torsion needs immediate surgery.
A high-risk score, ascites or a markedly raised CA-125 sends the patient to a gynecologic oncologist before surgery, because intact removal and staging at the first operation decide the outcome.

CA-125 comes from coelomic-type epithelium, so endometriosis, fibroids, pelvic infection, pregnancy and menstruation raise it. In a premenopausal woman a high value is **nonspecific**, and it stays normal in about half of early-stage cancers. It helps most in a postmenopausal woman with a complex mass and for following a known epithelial cancer.
Why does an enlarged ovary twist, and what dies first?

In ovarian **torsion** the ovary rotates on the infundibulopelvic (suspensory) ligament, which carries the ovarian vessels, and on the utero-ovarian ligament. A heavy ovary, usually one enlarged by a dermoid or a cyst of 5 cm or more, is the lever, although a normal ovary can twist in a girl. The story is sudden, severe, one-sided pelvic pain with nausea and vomiting. Veins and lymphatics collapse first, so the ovary swells with **venous** congestion before arterial flow stops and **hemorrhagic infarction** follows; Doppler flow can persist early, so normal flow does not exclude torsion.
How torsion destroys an ovary, step by step
An ovary enlarged by a dermoid or cyst swings on its ligaments and twists the pedicle that carries its vessels.
Low-pressure, thin-walled veins and lymphatics are squeezed shut while arterial blood still enters, so the ovary becomes congested and edematous.
Rising tissue pressure and further twisting finally stop arterial inflow, so an early Doppler study can still show flow.
Without inflow the ovary infarcts; prompt laparoscopic detorsion, even of a dark, swollen ovary, usually preserves function.
Which cell did the tumor come from?

Ovarian tumors are classified by the normal cell they resemble, because each of the ovary's three cell types, with its own embryologic origin, keeps its own behavior when it turns neoplastic. The surface epithelium derives from the **coelomic epithelium** covering the genital ridge. It dips into the stroma as inclusion cysts and takes on Müllerian-type (tubal, endometrial or endocervical) differentiation, which is why its tumors are called serous, endometrioid and mucinous. It gives rise to about 90 percent of malignant ovarian tumors, mostly in older women, although many high-grade serous carcinomas actually begin in the fallopian tube and seed the ovary.

**Primordial germ cells** arise in the yolk sac wall and reach the genital ridge in the fifth to sixth week, so germ cell tumors are the common ovarian neoplasms of girls and young women, and stray germ cells explain the same tumors in the midline outside the ovary. **Sex cord**-stromal cells (granulosa, theca, Sertoli and Leydig cells and fibroblasts) come from genital ridge mesenchyme and give tumors that often make hormones. Metastases make a fourth group, such as the {{rp15_kruk|Krukenberg tumor}}: bilateral ovarian masses of mucin-secreting signet-ring cells, usually from a gastric primary.

Epithelial tumors run from benign to borderline to malignant. **Serous** tumors are the most common; they are often bilateral, and psammoma bodies (concentric calcifications) are common but not specific. **Mucinous** tumors can grow very large as mucin-filled, multiloculated cystic masses; they are usually unilateral with a KRAS mutation, so bilateral mucinous masses suggest metastasis from the appendix or gut. Pseudomyxoma peritonei, a belly full of gelatinous mucin, usually comes from an appendiceal tumor. Endometrioid and clear cell carcinomas arise from endometriosis. The **Brenner tumor** has transitional-type nests with coffee-bean nuclei and is usually benign. A {{rp15_bord|borderline tumor}} has stratification and atypia without destructive stromal invasion, and its peritoneal implants are usually noninvasive, so most patients do well.

Carcinomas follow two paths. Type I carcinomas (low-grade serous, mucinous, endometrioid and clear cell) grow slowly from borderline tumors or endometriosis, driven by KRAS, BRAF or PTEN changes. Type II is **high-grade serous carcinoma**, the most common and most lethal ovarian cancer. It starts as {{rp15_stic|serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma}} in the fimbriated end of the tube, carries an early TP53 mutation, and is the ovarian cancer of BRCA1 and BRCA2 carriers. It sheds cells onto peritoneal surfaces, so women present late with bloating, early satiety and rising girth from ascites and **omental** caking, with a raised CA-125. Treatment is staging with cytoreductive (debulking) surgery and platinum chemotherapy, plus PARP inhibitors for BRCA carriers.
TP53 in nearly all; often BRCA1 or BRCA2
Slow; often confined to the ovary
Who is at risk of ovarian cancer, and what protects?

About 5 to 10 percent of ovarian cancers are hereditary. Germline BRCA1 or BRCA2 variants raise lifetime risk to roughly 40 to 60 percent for BRCA1 and 10 to 20 percent for BRCA2, against 1 to 2 percent in the general population, almost always as high-grade serous carcinoma. Lynch syndrome, a mismatch repair defect, adds endometrioid and clear cell carcinoma to its colon and endometrial cancers. Other risks are older age, **nulliparity**, early menarche, late menopause, endometriosis and, for mucinous tumors, smoking. Protective factors are oral contraceptives (five or more years cut risk by about half), pregnancy and multiparity, breastfeeding, and tubal ligation or salpingectomy.
Why do oral contraceptives and tubal surgery lower ovarian cancer risk?

Each ovulation breaks the ovarian surface and bathes the nearby fimbriae in follicular fluid full of inflammatory mediators, and the repair needs cell division that can copy DNA errors. Anything that cuts lifetime ovulations therefore lowers risk: oral contraceptives, pregnancy and multiparity, and breastfeeding, while nulliparity, early menarche and late menopause raise it. Tubal ligation and salpingectomy protect for a second reason: most high-grade serous carcinomas begin in the fimbriated tube, so removing or isolating the tube removes the cells that start the cancer. That is why salpingectomy is now offered instead of tubal ligation.
No screening test works for average-risk women

Large trials of yearly CA-125 and transvaginal ultrasound did not lower ovarian cancer deaths, and false positives caused needless surgery, so the USPSTF recommends against screening average-risk women (as of 2025). Prevention targets high-risk women: BRCA carriers are offered risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy after childbearing, at 35 to 40 years for BRCA1 and 40 to 45 for BRCA2, which also removes any tubal STIC.
Which tumors announce themselves with a marker or a hormone?

Germ cell tumors are named for the tissue they imitate. The mature cystic **teratoma**, or dermoid cyst, is the most common ovarian neoplasm in young women; it is benign, holds hair, teeth and sebum from all three germ layers, and is heavy enough to cause torsion. Struma ovarii, a teratoma of mostly thyroid tissue, can cause hyperthyroidism, and an immature teratoma contains immature neuroepithelium and is malignant. The **dysgerminoma**, the counterpart of seminoma, forms sheets of large clear cells with lymphocyte-rich septa, raises lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), is very radiosensitive, and arises more often in gonadal dysgenesis with Y chromosome material (Swyer syndrome, some Turner mosaics). The **yolk sac tumor** of girls and young women makes alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and shows glomerulus-like {{rp15_sd|Schiller-Duval bodies}}; choriocarcinoma makes human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) from trophoblast without villi.

Sex cord-stromal tumors act like the cells they came from. The **granulosa cell tumor** makes estrogen: in a young girl it causes precocious puberty, and in an older woman unopposed estrogen causes endometrial hyperplasia, endometrial cancer and postmenopausal bleeding, so an endometrial biopsy belongs in the work-up. Its cells have grooved coffee-bean nuclei around small follicle-like {{rp15_ce|Call-Exner bodies}}, and inhibin is its serum marker. The **Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor** makes androgens, so a young woman develops hirsutism, a deeper voice and clitoromegaly.

The thecoma makes estrogen, and the fibroma makes no hormone but can cause **Meigs syndrome**: an ovarian fibroma with ascites and a right pleural effusion, all of which resolve once the tumor is removed. Molecular clues are few: most adult granulosa cell tumors carry a FOXL2 mutation, Sertoli-Leydig tumors cluster in DICER1 syndrome, and Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (STK11) predisposes to sex cord tumors with annular tubules.
How do the five gynecologic cancers differ by site?

The risk factor usually names the gynecologic cancer. Estrogen unopposed by progesterone, from obesity, anovulation, estrogen-only therapy or tamoxifen, drives the endometrium through hyperplasia to endometrioid carcinoma. Persistent high-risk HPV causes cervical, many vulvar and some vaginal cancers: the viral oncoprotein **E6** degrades p53 and E7 inactivates Rb, and immunosuppression (HIV, transplant) and smoking let infection persist. HPV-negative vulvar cancer arises on lichen sclerosus in older women, and diethylstilbestrol (DES) exposure in utero leaves vaginal adenosis, the soil of clear cell adenocarcinoma.
Tubal STIC to high-grade serous carcinoma
CA-125 and ultrasound; staging, cytoreduction, platinum
Atypical hyperplasia to endometrioid carcinoma; serous (TP53) in atrophy
Dysplasia (CIN) to squamous carcinoma via E6 and E7
Colposcopy with biopsy; conization for CIN; hysterectomy or chemoradiation
Vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia (HPV type or differentiated, TP53) to squamous carcinoma
Biopsy; wide local excision with sentinel node biopsy
Adenosis to clear cell adenocarcinoma; HPV squamous carcinoma; sarcoma botryoides (infants)
Biopsy; radiation, or surgery and chemotherapy for sarcoma botryoides

body.q: A 19-year-old has a solid ovarian mass and a markedly raised serum AFP. Which reasoning best identifies the tumor?
o: AFP is made by epithelial ovarian cancers, so a serous carcinoma is most likely
A raised marker means hormone production, so the tumor is of sex cord-stromal origin
AFP comes from trophoblast, so the mass is most likely a choriocarcinoma
AFP is a yolk sac protein, so a germ cell tumor imitating yolk sac is most likely
body.why: Each germ cell tumor secretes the protein of the tissue it imitates. Embryonic yolk sac makes alpha-fetoprotein, so a yolk sac tumor raises AFP and shows Schiller-Duval bodies. Trophoblast makes hCG, so choriocarcinoma raises hCG, and dysgerminoma raises LDH. Epithelial cancers raise CA-125, and sex cord-stromal tumors make steroid hormones and inhibin.
